summary: The lowlands, glaciers and long fjord south of Longyearbyen: Reindalen, the largest ice-free valley on Spitsbergen, the seabird cliffs of Ingeborgfjellet on the Bellsund coast, and Van Mijenfjorden itself, whose winter ice is protected for the animals that depend on it. The park began in 2003 as Nordenskiöld Land National Park and was more than tripled in size in 2021, after coal mining at Sveagruva came to an end.
story: Van Mijenfjorden runs 83 kilometres into Spitsbergen between Nordenskiöld Land and Nathorst Land, and the long, narrow island of Akseløya all but closes its mouth. The park takes in the fjord, the southern half of Nordenskiöld Land and the land across the water to Van Keulenfjorden. Its heart is Reindalen, about 38 kilometres long and the largest of Spitsbergen's ice-free valleys; at its mouth the rivers spread across the wet plain of Stormyra, part of one of Svalbard's largest river deltas. The fjord's name is a slip of the pen: it honours the Dutchman Willem Van Muyden, whose name A. E. Nordenskiöld misspelt.

The park protects large areas of lush, continuous vegetation, an interesting moss flora and wide wetlands. Nordenskiöld Land has the densest population of Svalbard reindeer in the archipelago, and Arctic foxes range across the coastal plain. On the Bellsund coast the cliffs of Ingeborgfjellet hold large colonies of little auks, Brünnich's guillemots and kittiwakes, and the coastal plain of Nordenskiöldkysten is a Ramsar wetland of international importance. The inner fjord and Van Keulenfjorden, with the bays of Rindersbukta and Fridtjovhamna, are protected as important habitat for animals that depend on sea ice.

People came for what the land could yield. Trappers wintered on these shores, and in the early twentieth century prospectors built camps on the Bellsund coast — Camp Bell, where Ernest Mansfield wintered in 1908–09, and Camp Millar, put up in 1910. In 1917 Swedes opened a coal mine at Sveagruva, at the head of the fjord; the Norwegian company Store Norske bought it in 1934 and worked it, with long breaks, until mining ended in 2020. Almost every building at Svea has since been removed.

Nordenskiöld Land National Park was created in 2003 to protect Reindalen and the coast to the west, 1,337 square kilometres of land and sea. In June 2021, the year after the mines closed, it was enlarged to 4,251 square kilometres and renamed Van Mijenfjorden National Park. The new regulation let the clean-up of the old mining areas at Svea and Lunckefjell be finished inside the park, closed parts of Midterhuken, Eholmen and Mariaholmen in summer and banned most motor traffic on the fjord ice after 1 March. Since 2025 tourist landings have been limited, drones banned and ships with more than 200 passengers barred.
howItWorks: Svalbard has its own law, the Svalbard Environmental Protection Act. The public right of access applies here too, but all travel must leave no damage, litter or needless disturbance. Polar bears are protected: no one may disturb, attract or pursue one, or come closer than 300 metres — 500 metres from 1 March to 30 June — and anyone who finds a bear inside that distance must withdraw. Everyone outside the settlements, apart from people on an organised tour, must know how to guard against a polar bear attack and carry the means to scare a bear off. Everything people left before 1946 is a protected monument with a 100-metre zone around it, where camping and fires are not allowed (a tent on frozen, snow-covered ground is the exception).

Since 1 January 2026 a field-safety regulation decides who must tell the Governor of Svalbard (Sysselmesteren) before setting out. The north side of the park — Reindalen, the Nordenskiöld Land coast and the fjord itself — lies inside the 'travel area' drawn around Isfjorden, where an independent visitor need not notify the Governor. On the south side of Van Mijenfjorden the travel area reaches only 500 metres inland from the shore, and Van Keulenfjorden lies beyond it: to go there, notify the Governor four weeks ahead and wait for the reply, carry equipment to raise the alarm and talk both ways, and hold insurance or a guarantee for search and rescue of up to NOK 120,000 per operation. Tour operators need the Governor's permission for all their trips.

The park's regulation bans cycling on bare ground, drones, aircraft landings and flying lower than 300 metres within a nautical mile of land, and ships carrying more than 200 passengers. Tourist landings are allowed only on frozen, snow-covered ground from 1 January to 25 May, or within a designated landing area, and always with a guide. Marked areas on Midterhuken and the islets of Eholmen and Mariaholmen are closed to all traffic from 15 May to 15 August. Under Svalbard's motor-traffic rules, visitors may drive snowmobiles on frozen, snow-covered ground on the Nordenskiöld Land side, but after 1 March not on the ice of Van Mijenfjorden or Van Keulenfjorden, except by the shortest route to a cabin or, on an organised tour, along the north shore of Van Mijenfjorden.

sights.name: Reindalen
sights.note: The largest ice-free valley on Spitsbergen, about 38 kilometres long, opening onto the wet delta plain of Stormyra and the bay of Kaldbukta.

sights.name: Stormyra
sights.note: A wet plain about seven kilometres across at the mouth of Reindalen, where several rivers braid their way to the bay of Kaldbukta.

sights.name: Ingeborgfjellet
sights.note: A 714-metre mountain on the Bellsund coast whose cliffs hold colonies of little auks, Brünnich's guillemots and kittiwakes.

sights.name: Fridtjovhamna
sights.note: A bay on the outer north shore of Van Mijenfjorden, left behind as the glacier Fridtjovbreen retreated; key ground for ice-dependent animals.

sights.name: Akseløya
sights.note: An island 8.5 kilometres long and about a kilometre wide that lies across the mouth of Van Mijenfjorden, leaving only narrow sounds on either side.

sights.name: Midterhuken
sights.note: The mountain headland between Bellsund's two arms, Van Mijenfjorden and Van Keulenfjorden. Marked areas on it are closed to all traffic from 15 May to 15 August.

sights.name: Rindersbukta
sights.note: The southern inner arm of Van Mijenfjorden, below the glaciers Scheelebreen and Paulabreen; named after the Dutch whaling skipper Michiel Rinders.

entrances: Overland from Longyearbyen into Reindalen and along the Nordenskiöld Land coast — by snowmobile on frozen, snowy ground in winter and spring, on foot in summer
By boat through Bellsund, past Akseløya, into Van Mijenfjorden when the water is open
planYourVisit.reservations: No notification is needed for an independent trip on the Nordenskiöld Land side or on the fjord, which lie inside the travel area around Isfjorden. Trips into Nathorst Land beyond the shore, or to Van Keulenfjorden, must be notified to the Governor of Svalbard four weeks ahead. Operators in Longyearbyen, licensed by the Governor, run guided trips.
permits: Notification to the Governor four weeks ahead for travel outside the travel area, with search-and-rescue insurance of up to NOK 120,000 per operation
A rifle for polar bear protection can be hired only from a licensed dealer, and only by someone holding a Norwegian firearms licence, a European firearms pass or a loan permit from the Governor
Camping in one place for a week or more needs the Governor's permission
camping: Wild camping, on bare ground where possible, at least 100 metres from cabins and outside the 100-metre zone around protected monuments (a tent on frozen, snow-covered ground excepted)
Every camp must keep flare guns, signal pens or other means of scaring off polar bears close at hand
lodging: None in the park; Longyearbyen is the nearest town
seasonalClosures: Marked areas on Midterhuken, Eholmen and Mariaholmen are closed to all traffic from 15 May to 15 August

After 1 March snowmobiles may not travel on the ice of Van Mijenfjorden or Van Keulenfjorden, except by the shortest route to a cabin or, on an organised tour, along the north shore of Van Mijenfjorden
Outside the designated landing area, tourist landings are allowed only on frozen, snow-covered ground from 1 January to 25 May

weather: Svalbard's climate is Arctic but milder than its latitude suggests, because the last of the North Atlantic Current warms the west coast. Inland valleys such as Reindalen run a couple of degrees warmer than the coast in summer and a few degrees colder in winter. Summer means are only about 4–7 °C and January means around −9 to −13 °C, and snow can fall in any month. At Longyearbyen the midnight sun lasts from about 20 April to late August and the polar night from late October to mid-February. Svalbard has warmed several times faster than the world as a whole since the 1970s.
directions: Fly to Svalbard Airport, Longyear, which has daily scheduled flights from Oslo and Tromsø. No roads link Longyearbyen to the rest of Spitsbergen. The Nordenskiöld Land side of the park lies inside the zone where visitors may drive snowmobiles on frozen, snow-covered ground, so in winter and spring it can be reached overland from Longyearbyen, independently or on a guided tour. In summer motor traffic over land is banned, and the way in is on foot or by boat through Bellsund.

fees.title: Svalbard environmental fee
fees.detail: Paid by every visitor to Svalbard except residents: collected with the ticket for the flight out of Svalbard, or by the travel organiser. It goes to the Svalbard Environmental Protection Fund.

chronology.text: The prospector Ernest Mansfield builds Camp Bell on the Bellsund coast and winters there; Camp Millar follows in 1910.
Swedes open a coal mine at Sveagruva, at the head of Van Mijenfjorden.
The Norwegian company Store Norske buys Sveagruva.
Nordenskiöld Land National Park is created on 26 September to protect Reindalen and the coast to the west.
The coastal plain of Nordenskiöldkysten, with the bird cliffs of Ingeborgfjellet, is listed as a Ramsar wetland of international importance.
Coal mining at Svea ends; almost every building is later removed and the land restored.
The park is enlarged to 4,251 square kilometres and renamed Van Mijenfjorden National Park; parts of Midterhuken close in summer, and most motor traffic on the fjord ice is banned after 1 March.
Tourist landings are limited to a designated area and frozen ground, drones are banned, and ships with more than 200 passengers are barred.
A new field-safety regulation takes effect; the park's north side lies inside its travel area.

safety: Polar bears can appear anywhere, at any time of year, on land or on the fjord ice. Keep a constant lookout, carry the means to scare a bear off, and know how to use them.
Reindalen's braided rivers rise with summer meltwater and can be dangerous to wade. Look for a crossing where the channels spread widest and shallowest, and turn back if in doubt.
Sea ice can be thin or break up without warning. Ask locally about conditions before going out on Van Mijenfjorden, and remember the ban on driving on its ice after 1 March.
Weather turns fast, and winter whiteouts erase the landscape. Carry navigation, warm clothing, food for longer than planned and a way to call for help.
regulations: Keep at least 300 metres from polar bears, and 500 metres from 1 March to 30 June.
Drones are banned, and aircraft may not land or fly lower than 300 metres within a nautical mile of land.
Cycling on bare ground is banned, and snowmobiles are allowed only on frozen, snow-covered ground.
Marked areas on Midterhuken, Eholmen and Mariaholmen are closed to all traffic from 15 May to 15 August.

Ships with more than 200 passengers may not enter the park's waters, and tourist landings are allowed only with a guide, in the designated area or on frozen, snow-covered ground from 1 January to 25 May.
